title: Compound nouns (smikhut)
topic: the construct state: בֵּית סֵפֶר, כּוֹס קָפֶה
why: Smikhut, or the construct state, joins two nouns into one: it's how Hebrew says "school," "breakfast," or "bus stop." You learn when the first noun changes form and where to put the article, and you'll see that the word order is the reverse of English compound nouns.

{"lessons": ["

Two nouns stuck together: smikhut

In English, you say \"a cup of coffee.\" In Hebrew, you simply put the two nouns side by side, with no \"of\": כּוֹס קָפֶה (kos kafe). This is smikhut, the construct state.

כּוֹס קָפֶהa cup of coffee [kos kafe]
מִיץ תַּפּוּזִיםorange juice, word for word \"juice (of) oranges\" [mits tapuzim]
בֵּית סֵפֶרa school, word for word \"house (of) book\" [beit sefer]

The order is like \"a cup of coffee,\" not like an English compound: the main noun comes first, then the noun that describes it. So \"orange juice\" is literally \"juice oranges,\" and \"bus stop\" is \"stop bus.\" כּוֹס קָפֶה is a cup, not coffee.

You already know one smikhut: סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ (end of the week, the weekend), in בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ.

", "

The first noun sometimes changes

The second noun never moves. The first one, though, often takes a shorter form:

Noun aloneIn smikhutExample
בַּיִת bayitבֵּית beitבֵּית קָפֶה café (the place)
חֶדֶר khederחֲדַר khadarחֲדַר שֵׁנָה bedroom
אֲרוּחָה arukhaאֲרוּחַת arukhatאֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר breakfast
שָׂפָה safaשְׂפַת sfatשְׂפַת הַיָּם seashore
תַּחֲנָה takhanaתַּחֲנַת takhanatתַּחֲנַת אוֹטוֹבּוּס bus stop
מְסִבָּה mesibaמְסִבַּת mesibatמְסִבַּת יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת birthday party
כּוֹס kosכּוֹס kosכּוֹס מַיִם glass of water (no change)

The most useful rule: a feminine noun in ־ָה (a) ends in ־ַת (at). You hear an extra t: אֲרוּחָה → אֲרוּחַת.

In the masculine plural, ־ִים becomes ־ֵי: בָּתִּים → בָּתֵּי סֵפֶר (schools). For now, just recognize it.

", "

Where does the article go?

Here's the big trap. To say \"the school,\" the article הַ־ goes on the second noun, never on the first:

בֵּית הַסֵּפֶרthe school [beit ha-sefer]
אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶרthe breakfast [arukhat ha-boker]

In casual speech, you'll sometimes hear הַבֵּית סֵפֶר, but the correct form is בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר. A preposition attaches to the first noun, with no article: בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר (be-veit ha-sefer, at school), לְבֵית הַקָּפֶה (to the café).

The adjective comes at the very end and agrees with the first noun: אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר טוֹבָה (a good breakfast), because אֲרוּחָה is feminine. With the article: בֵּית הַקָּפֶה הַקָּטָן (the little café).

In בְּבֵית, the second ב has no dot: it's read v, be-veit.
